topic.title: PostgreSQL
topic.description: psql, diagnostics queries, locks, maintenance, backup and restore (PostgreSQL 16)

commands.name: psql
commands.description: Connects to a PostgreSQL server, runs SQL and provides backslash meta-commands for inspection.

examples.scenario: Connect to database appdb on db.internal as user app.

examples.scenario: Print the server version from a script, without opening the shell.

examples.scenario: Execute migration.sql against appdb.

use_cases.title: Ad-hoc diagnosis
use_cases.situation: Open a session to inspect activity, locks and sizes during an incident.

pitfalls: Use ~/.pgpass instead of typing passwords on the command line (they end up in shell history).

commands.name: psql meta-commands
commands.summary: Backslash commands to inspect databases inside psql
commands.description: psql-only commands (not SQL) that list databases, tables, indexes, roles and toggle output options.

flags.description: Show execution time of each query.

examples.title: List databases
examples.scenario: Inside psql, list every database with owner and encoding.

examples.title: Tables with sizes
examples.scenario: List tables in the current database including their sizes.

examples.title: Describe a table
examples.scenario: Show columns, indexes and constraints of the orders table.

examples.title: List roles
examples.scenario: Which roles exist and what attributes do they have?

examples.title: Measure query time
examples.scenario: Turn on timing so each query prints its duration.

examples.title: Switch database
examples.scenario: From the current session, connect to the reporting database.

use_cases.title: Unknown schema
use_cases.situation: Explore an unfamiliar database before writing queries.

commands.name: pg_isready
commands.summary: Check whether the server accepts connections
commands.description: Returns the connection status of a server via exit code; ideal for health checks and scripts.

examples.title: Remote readiness
examples.scenario: Is db.internal accepting connections on port 5432?

output_notes.anomaly: rejecting connections (1, e.g. starting up) or no response (2).

use_cases.title: Startup ordering
use_cases.situation: Wait in a script until the database is ready before starting the app.

commands.name: pg_stat_activity
commands.summary: One row per server process: who is running what
commands.description: System view with each connection's user, application, state, current query and wait event.

flags.description: What the backend waits for (Lock, IO, Client…).

examples.title: Running queries
examples.scenario: List PID, user and query of every active backend.
examples.command: SELECT pid, usename, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state = 'active';

examples.title: Queries running longer than 5 minutes
examples.scenario: Find active queries running for more than 5 minutes.
examples.command:
SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS age, query FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active' AND now() - query_start > interval '5 minutes';

examples.title: Idle in transaction
examples.scenario: List sessions stuck 'idle in transaction', which hold locks and block vacuum.
examples.command:
SELECT pid, usename, xact_start FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle in transaction';

examples.title: Connections per state
examples.scenario: Count connections grouped by state to spot connection leaks.
examples.command: SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state;

use_cases.title: Database slow for everyone
use_cases.situation: Look for long queries or many sessions waiting on locks.

use_cases.title: Too many connections
use_cases.situation: Find which application is leaking idle connections.

commands.name: pg_terminate_backend
commands.summary: Cancel a query or terminate a session
commands.description: pg_cancel_backend stops the current query; pg_terminate_backend closes the whole session and rolls back its transaction.

examples.title: Cancel a query
examples.scenario: Stop the query running in backend 4242 but keep its session.

examples.title: Terminate a session
examples.scenario: Backend 4242 is idle in transaction and blocking others. Terminate it.

use_cases.title: Runaway report query
use_cases.situation: Cancel a query saturating the server, then contact its owner.

pitfalls: Terminating rolls back the session's open transaction; prefer cancel first.

commands.name: pg_blocking_pids
commands.description: pg_blocking_pids(pid) returns the PIDs blocking a backend; combined with pg_stat_activity it shows lock chains.

examples.title: Blocked sessions and their blockers
examples.scenario: List every waiting backend with the PIDs that block it.
examples.command:
SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by, query
FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;

use_cases.title: Migration stuck
use_cases.situation: An ALTER TABLE waits for a lock held by a long transaction.

commands.name: EXPLAIN ANALYZE
commands.summary: Show and measure a query plan
commands.description: EXPLAIN prints the planner's chosen plan; ANALYZE executes the query and adds real timings and row counts.

flags.description: Run the query and report actual time and rows.
Show shared buffer hits and reads.

examples.title: Measure a slow query
examples.scenario: See the real plan and timing of the lookup of customer 42's orders.
examples.command: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
examples.output:
Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..18334.00 rows=96 width=64) (actual time=0.031..92.114 rows=104 loops=1)
  Filter: (customer_id = 42)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 999896
Execution Time: 92.201 ms

output_notes.anomaly: On a large table with a selective filter: missing index.
Huge: an index on the filter column would help.

examples.title: Plan without running
examples.scenario: Show the plan of a DELETE without executing it.
examples.command: EXPLAIN DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < now();

use_cases.title: Slow endpoint
use_cases.situation: Confirm a missing index before adding it.

pitfalls: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement: wrap writes in BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK;.

commands.name: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
commands.summary: Build an index without blocking writes
commands.synopsis: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY name ON table (column);
commands.description: Builds an index while allowing inserts, updates and deletes; slower than a plain build and cannot run inside a transaction.

examples.title: Index on a busy table
examples.scenario: Add an index on orders(customer_id) without blocking writes.
examples.command: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer ON orders (customer_id);

examples.title: Indexes of a table
examples.scenario: List the index names and definitions of the orders table.
examples.command: SELECT indexname, indexdef FROM pg_indexes WHERE tablename = 'orders';

use_cases.title: Fix a seq scan in production
use_cases.situation: Add the missing index without downtime.

pitfalls: If a concurrent build fails, it leaves an INVALID index; drop it and retry.

commands.name: pg_size_pretty
commands.description: Size functions (pg_database_size, pg_total_relation_size) with pg_size_pretty for human-readable output.

examples.title: Size of the current database
examples.scenario: How big is the current database?

examples.title: Five largest tables
examples.scenario: List the five largest tables including indexes and TOAST.
examples.command:
SELECT relname, pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(relid))
FROM pg_statio_user_tables ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(relid) DESC LIMIT 5;

use_cases.title: Disk filling up
use_cases.situation: Find which tables grew before planning cleanup or archiving.

commands.name: VACUUM
commands.summary: Reclaim dead rows and refresh statistics
commands.description: Marks space of dead tuples reusable and, with ANALYZE, updates planner statistics. Autovacuum normally does this automatically.

flags.description: Rewrite the table to return space to the OS (exclusive lock).

examples.title: Vacuum and analyze one table
examples.scenario: After a large delete on orders, vacuum it and refresh its statistics.

examples.title: Tables with most dead rows
examples.scenario: Which tables have the most dead tuples and when were they last autovacuumed?
examples.command:
SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 5;

use_cases.title: Table bloat
use_cases.situation: A frequently updated table keeps growing despite a stable row count.

pitfalls: VACUUM FULL locks the table exclusively for the whole rewrite; avoid it during business hours.

flags.description: Custom compressed format (restorable selectively with pg_restore).

examples.title: Schema only

examples.title: One table

use_cases.title: Before a risky migration

commands.description: Restores dumps made with pg_dump -Fc, optionally into another database, selectively and in parallel.

examples.scenario: Restore appdb.dump into the existing database appdb_restore.

examples.title: Inspect a dump
examples.scenario: List what appdb.dump contains before restoring.

examples.title: Parallel restore
examples.scenario: Restore appdb.dump into appdb_restore using 4 jobs.

use_cases.title: Restore test
use_cases.situation: Prove backups are usable by restoring into a scratch database.

commands.name: CREATE ROLE / GRANT
commands.synopsis: CREATE ROLE name LOGIN PASSWORD '...'; GRANT ... ON ... TO name;
commands.description: Roles are users and groups; privileges are granted per database, schema and table.

examples.title: Create a login role
examples.scenario: Create a login role named report with a password.

examples.title: Read-only access to a schema
examples.scenario: Allow report to read every table in schema public.
examples.command: GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO report;

examples.title: Allow connecting
examples.scenario: Allow report to connect to database appdb.
examples.command: GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE appdb TO report;

use_cases.situation: Give an analytics tool read-only access without exposing the app user.

pitfalls: GRANT ... ON ALL TABLES covers existing tables only; use ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES for future ones.

procedures.title: Triage a database that is slow for everyone
procedures.context: All requests touching the database became slow a few minutes ago.
procedures.goal: Find long queries or lock waits and relieve the pressure.

steps.command: SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state;

SELECT pid, now() - query_start AS age, query FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'active' ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 5;

SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;
SELECT pg_cancel_backend(4242);
steps.interpretation: Escalate to pg_terminate_backend only if cancel does not help.

use_cases.title: Lock pile-up
use_cases.situation: One long transaction blocks dozens of updates.

procedures.title: Find and fix a missing index
procedures.context: The orders page takes seconds to load for some customers.
procedures.goal: Confirm a sequential scan and add an index without downtime.

steps.command: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
steps.interpretation: Seq Scan with many rows removed by filter.

steps.command: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer ON orders (customer_id);
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;
steps.output: Index Scan using idx_orders_customer on orders ... Execution Time: 0.180 ms

procedures.title: Back up and prove the restore works
procedures.context: Monthly check that backups of appdb are restorable.
procedures.goal: Dump, restore into a scratch database and compare row counts.

steps.command: pg_dump -U app -Fc -f appdb.dump appdb
createdb -U app appdb_restore
pg_restore -U app -j 4 -d appdb_restore appdb.dump
psql -U app -d appdb_restore -c "SELECT count(*) FROM orders;"

procedures.title: Investigate 'too many connections'
procedures.context: New connections fail with FATAL: sorry, too many clients already.
procedures.goal: Find the source of idle connections and free slots.

steps.command: SHOW max_connections;

SELECT application_name, state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY 3 DESC;
steps.interpretation: Many idle sessions from one app: missing pool or leak.

steps.command:
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(pid) FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state = 'idle' AND state_change < now() - interval '1 hour';

procedures.title: Create a read-only reporting user
procedures.context: The BI team needs read access to appdb without write privileges.
procedures.goal: Create the role, grant connect and read rights, including future tables.

steps.command: CREATE ROLE report LOGIN PASSWORD 'change-me';
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE appdb TO report;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO report;
GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO report;
ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT SELECT ON TABLES TO report;

procedures.title: Check and reduce table bloat
procedures.context: The events table keeps growing although old rows are deleted daily.
procedures.goal: Confirm dead tuples and vacuum the table.

steps.command:
SELECT relname, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum FROM pg_stat_user_tables
WHERE relname = 'events';
SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size('events'));
VACUUM (VERBOSE, ANALYZE) events;
steps.interpretation: Space becomes reusable inside the table; the file does not shrink without VACUUM FULL.
